chapterTitle: Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) with AWS CodePipeline and CodeBuild
aiGenerationNote: Create a 18-minute live coding and console walkthrough video. Start with a brief animated overview of CI/CD concepts and the roles of CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline. Transition to a terminal to demonstrate cloning a CodeCommit repository, adding `index.html` and a detailed `buildspec.yml` (including `install`, `pre_build`, `build`, `post_build` phases for a simple static site, with `artifacts` defined), and pushing to CodeCommit. Then, switch to the AWS console to create the CodeBuild project, linking it to CodeCommit and specifying the `buildspec.yml` and S3 artifact bucket. Show a manual CodeBuild run and review its logs. Finally, guide the learner through creating a multi-stage CodePipeline, connecting CodeCommit as the source, CodeBuild as the build stage, and the pre-existing CodeDeploy application (from Chapter 4.3) as the deploy stage. Show the pipeline execution, emphasizing the flow between stages. End with a demonstration of a code change triggering a full pipeline run and the updated application in the browser.

screens.title: CI/CD with AWS CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore how Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery reduce friction in software delivery by automatically building, testing, and preparing releases. You will learn what CI and CD mean in practice, how AWS CodeCommit stores your source, how CodeBuild compiles and tests, and how CodePipeline orchestrates stages from source to deploy. I will show a practical workflow that starts with a commit and ends with an automated deployment, and explain why artifacts, build specifications, and IAM roles are vital pieces that hold the pipeline together. You will see a concise hands-on example where a small static site is pushed, built, packaged, and delivered to an EC2 instance through CodeDeploy. Along the way we'll point out common pitfalls, like missing artifacts or incorrect IAM permissions, and how to check build logs when something fails. By the end you should understand the responsibility of each managed service and how a well-formed buildspec file enables reliable, repeatable builds. Think of this chapter as mapping the path from a developer's commit to a safe, repeatable release.

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: CI automates frequent integration with builds and tests; CD ensures built artifacts are always ready for deployment. AWS CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline provide a managed, end-to-end CI/CD flow.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › CI/CD Overview
CI/CD with AWS Managed Developer Tools
Build repeatable pipelines that turn commits into deployable artifacts.
Continuous Integration

Frequent merges trigger builds and tests so integration issues surface quickly.

Continuous Delivery

Managed Services

Pipeline Stages

Why this chapter matters
Automating build and release pipelines reduces manual errors, shortens feedback loops, and makes deployments repeatable. These skills are core for SysOps engineers who maintain reliable delivery processes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will explain the core ideas of Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery, configure AWS CodeCommit as a secure Git source, author a buildspec file that drives CodeBuild, assemble a multi-stage pipeline in CodePipeline, and monitor or troubleshoot executions and build failures. These objectives are practical: you won't just name services, you'll use CodeCommit to host code, create a CodeBuild project that runs tests and produces artifacts, and link those into a CodePipeline that automates releases. For example, configuring a buildspec file ensures every build follows the same install, pre-build, build and post-build steps so test results are consistent. Another objective is writing minimal IAM roles to allow CodeBuild and CodePipeline to read and write artifacts, which avoids common permission errors. Finally, you will learn monitoring patterns, such as checking CodeBuild logs for failing commands and inspecting the pipeline stage history when a run halts. These skills make deployments predictable and reduce downtime during releases.

screens.title: What is Continuous Integration (CI) versus Continuous Delivery (CD)?
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Integration is a development practice where developers frequently merge code changes into a shared repository so an automated build and test suite runs on every merge. The key benefit is fast feedback: integration defects surface quickly when small changes are validated often. Continuous Delivery builds on CI by ensuring that every successful build produces a packaged artifact ready for deployment, so the application is always in a deployable state. In other words, CI answers the question 'Does the code integrate correctly?', while CD answers 'Can this build be safely released to production?'. A practical example is a team that pushes daily updates to a central repository: CI runs tests on each push; CD packages the successful build and makes it available to deployment stages. A common misconception is thinking CI alone equals automated releases; CI only verifies integration, while CD adds the packaging and delivery guarantees. Keep in mind that both practices reduce risk, but CD requires extra steps such as artifact management and deployment automation. To test your grasp, ask: after a passing build, how quickly could you deploy the produced artifact if needed?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CI gives fast integration feedback via automated builds and tests. CD ensures artifacts are packaged and release-ready so deployments are routine.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › CI vs CD
Definitions

Continuous Integration: Frequent merges to a central repo with automated builds and tests to catch integration problems early.

Continuous Delivery: All successful builds are packaged and ready for deployment, making releases routine and low-risk.

Analogy
Think of CI as quality checks in a factory line, and CD as boxed products staged at shipping so orders can be dispatched immediately.
Concrete Example
A developer pushes a feature branch; the pipeline runs unit tests and static checks. If they pass, CodeBuild creates an artifact and the pipeline marks the build ready for a deploy stage that can be triggered automatically or manually.
Common Misconception
CI does not imply automatic production deployment. CI focuses on integration and test validation; CD adds packaging and release automation to make deployment safe and repeatable.
Key Takeaway

Separate the goals: CI gives immediate integration feedback; CD keeps artifacts release-ready so you can deploy with confidence.

screens.title: Roles of CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline
screens.narratorSegment: AWS provides a managed trio that covers source control, build automation, and orchestration. CodeCommit is the Git-compatible repository that acts as the single source of truth for your code and buildspec files. CodeBuild consumes that source, runs a build environment, executes the commands you author in a buildspec file, and produces artifacts such as a zipped application bundle. CodePipeline wires these pieces together: it defines stages and actions, monitors repository changes, and moves artifacts from source to build, test and deploy stages. A concrete example is when a developer pushes code with a buildspec at the repository root: CodePipeline detects the change, invokes CodeBuild which runs install and test commands and uploads the output artifact to S3. CodePipeline then triggers the deploy action to send the artifact to CodeDeploy or another deployment mechanism. A common mistake is treating CodePipeline as a build server; it is an orchestrator and relies on build services or actions to do the actual compile and test work. Remember to think in terms of artifacts flowing between stages; each service has a focused responsibility that together creates a robust CI/CD flow.

keyIdea.title: Service Roles
keyIdea.text: CodeCommit stores source, CodeBuild executes builds/tests and produces artifacts, CodePipeline orchestrates stages and passes artifacts along.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Tool Roles
Orchestration Architecture
SC
AWS CodeCommit — Source
A managed Git store that holds your application code and buildspec files. Acts as the reliable source for pipeline triggers.
CB
AWS CodeBuild — Build & Test
Runs build containers, executes install/test/build commands, and uploads artifacts to S3 for downstream stages.
CP
AWS CodePipeline — Orchestration
Defines stages and actions, passes artifacts, and monitors pipeline execution with automatic stops on failures.
Artifact Flow
Source code → CodeBuild executes buildspec → artifacts stored in S3 → CodePipeline moves artifacts to Deploy stage. Each arrow indicates an action producing an output artifact used by the next action.
Misconfiguration to Avoid
A frequent error is forgetting to include artifacts in the buildspec artifact section, resulting in empty output passed to downstream stages.
Key Takeaway

Treat each service as a single responsibility: source, build, and orchestrate. Correctly defining artifacts lets the pipeline move work forward without surprises.

screens.title: Understanding buildspec.yml
screens.narratorSegment: The buildspec file is the contract that tells CodeBuild how to build and package your project. It is a YAML file placed at the repository root and typically declares the version, phases such as install, pre_build, build and post_build, and an artifacts section that lists files to keep. A clear buildspec reduces flakiness by ensuring the build environment runs the same commands every time. For example, for a Node. js app you specify a node runtime, run dependency installation in install, run tests in pre_build, compile in build, and package outputs in post_build. A common mistake is leaving out the base-directory or the files pattern in artifacts, which results in no files being passed downstream. Another pitfall is assuming the build environment includes global tools; you should install or configure needed tools in the install phase. To validate a buildspec, run a test build in CodeBuild and inspect the logs line-by-line. In short, treat buildspec. yml as an exact script for reproducible builds and verify artifact paths to ensure pipeline continuity. Understanding buildspec.yml means buildspec.yml scripts the build environment and the artifact outputs; correct phase commands and artifact patterns are essential for reliable pipelines.. In practical terms, phases, artifacts, and why structure matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › buildspec.yml
Structure & Phases
  • version: Buildspec format version.
  • phases: install, pre_build, build, post_build — sequence of commands executed by CodeBuild.
  • artifacts: Files and base-directory to pass to the next pipeline stage.
Why this matters
A mis-specified artifacts section leads to empty downstream payloads. Missing install commands cause builds to fail due to absent dependencies.
Example buildspec.yml
version: 0.2

phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      nodejs: 18
    commands:
      - echo Installing dependencies...
      - npm install
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - echo Running tests...
      - npm test
  build:
    commands:
      - echo Building application...
      - npm run build
  post_build:
    commands:
      - echo Packaging artifacts...
artifacts:
  files:
    - '**/*'
  base-directory: build
Check your build
Run a test build and read logs: confirm install outputs, test pass/fail lines, and that the expected files appear in the build output. If artifacts are missing, re-check base-directory and file patterns.
Key Takeaway

A proper buildspec makes builds reproducible. Validate phases and artifact paths in a test build before wiring the pipeline to production stages.

screens.title: Creating a Basic CI/CD Pipeline — Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Constructing a pipeline means defining stages and actions that move artifacts from source to deployment. The minimal pipeline has three stages: Source, Build, and Deploy. First, create a CodeCommit repository and push your application and buildspec file. Next, create a CodeBuild project configured to use that repository and the buildspec file; set artifacts to an S3 bucket. Finally, create a CodePipeline pipeline that uses CodeCommit as the source action, your CodeBuild project as the build action, and a deploy action such as CodeDeploy pointing at an existing application and deployment group. A concrete CLI example is creating a repository with the cloud CLI and then cloning locally to push code; after pushing, CodePipeline will detect changes and trigger the build. A frequent oversight is not assigning service roles with permissions for S3 or CodeCommit; the pipeline will fail with permission denied errors. After creating the pipeline, trigger a change and observe the execution in the pipeline console. The pipeline will stop on failure, giving you the exact stage and action to investigate. Ask: are artifacts reaching S3 as expected before the deploy stage runs?

keyIdea.title: Pipeline Steps
keyIdea.text: A pipeline wires Source, Build, and Deploy stages. Ensure build artifacts are stored and accessible for the deploy stage and that roles have correct permissions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Pipeline Steps
Step-by-Step
1. Source
Create CodeCommit repo and push code including buildspec.yml. This is the pipeline trigger.
2. Build
Create CodeBuild project that consumes the repo and uploads artifacts to S3 according to buildspec artifacts section.
3. Deploy
Add a deploy action such as CodeDeploy to update your target environment with the artifact.
CLI Example
aws codecommit create-repository --repository-name MySimpleWebAppRepo --repository-description "My simple web app"
After creating a repository, clone it, add your files, commit, and push to trigger the pipeline flow.
Common Mistake
Forgetting to include buildspec.yml at the repository root or mis-setting artifact paths will stop the pipeline because downstream actions have nothing to consume.
Key Takeaway

Follow the source, build, deploy sequence and verify artifacts and IAM roles before expecting a successful end-to-end run.

screens.title: Artifacts and S3 — Passing Outputs Between Stages
screens.narratorSegment: Artifacts are the tangible outputs of build steps: compiled code, packages, Docker images, or static web files. In AWS pipelines, CodeBuild produces artifacts according to the buildspec's artifacts section and typically uploads them to an S3 artifact bucket. CodePipeline actions consume those artifacts as inputs for subsequent stages. For example, CodeBuild might package a site into a zip file and place it in a named S3 bucket; the deploy action then references that artifact to update the target environment. A common error is misconfiguring the artifacts. files or base-directory in buildspec. yml so the expected files are not included, resulting in empty inputs for the deploy stage. Another gotcha is S3 permissions: ensure the pipeline and build roles can write to and read from the artifact bucket. When diagnosing issues, verify the S3 bucket contains the expected artifact after a successful build and examine the pipeline execution history to confirm the artifact version passed along. Clear artifact paths and permissions keep stages connected and deployments reliable. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Artifacts & S3
What Are Artifacts?

Outputs of builds or tests that are consumed by later stages, such as zip bundles, compiled binaries, or static site files.

CodeBuild uploads artifacts to an S3 artifact bucket which CodePipeline references for downstream actions.

Verification
After a build, check the artifact bucket in S3 to confirm the expected archive or files exist. Then confirm the pipeline used that artifact version in the next stage.
Common Error
If artifacts.files uses an incorrect pattern, the artifact will be empty. If base-directory is wrong, CodeBuild will upload the wrong folder. Both lead to downstream failures.
Permissions
Ensure CodeBuild and CodePipeline service roles can read and write to the artifact S3 bucket. Lack of permissions will cause stage failures even if the build succeeds locally.

screens.title: IAM Roles for CodeBuild and CodePipeline
screens.narratorSegment: IAM roles let managed services perform actions on your behalf. CodeBuild needs a service role that allows it to pull source from CodeCommit, write artifacts to S3, and, if necessary, push images to ECR. CodePipeline needs permissions to access source, read artifacts, and invoke deploy actions. The simplest approach for learning is to attach managed policies that provide the needed actions, then later narrow permissions to least privilege in production. A frequent troubleshooting scenario is an otherwise successful build that fails when uploading artifacts because the CodeBuild role lacks S3 permissions. Another is CodePipeline failing to start because its role cannot read the repository or artifacts. To debug, review the IAM role attached to the service in the console and check CloudTrail or the pipeline's failure message for an AccessDenied indicator. Always avoid using overly broad policies in production; start broad to verify functionality, then remove unneeded permissions to achieve least privilege. IAM Roles for CodeBuild and CodePipeline means assign distinct service roles to codebuild and codepipeline with permissions for codecommit, s3, and deployment targets. start permissive for tests, then tighten to least privilege.. In practical terms, least-privilege essentials and common permission failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › IAM Roles
Role Responsibilities
  • CodeBuild role: Pull source, read secrets if needed, write artifacts to S3, push images to ECR if applicable.
  • CodePipeline role: Read source, access artifact store, invoke build and deploy actions.
Debugging Permissions
When a stage fails with AccessDenied, inspect the service role attached to that action and check if required policies (S3, CodeCommit, CodeBuild invocation) are present.
Practical Tip
For initial setup, attach managed policies to accelerate testing. After successful runs, reduce permissions to only the necessary S3 prefixes, repository ARNs, and specific deploy actions.
Key Takeaway

Service roles are the plumbing of pipelines. Review roles when a stage reports an access error and tighten permissions once functionality is verified.

screens.title: Monitoring and Troubleshooting Pipeline Executions
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring pipeline health requires looking at the right places: the CodePipeline console for the high-level execution flow and the CodeBuild logs for command-level detail. When a pipeline run fails at a stage, the pipeline console tells you which action failed and often includes an error summary. For build failures, open the CodeBuild build details and read the full logs to see which phase and command produced the error. For missing artifacts, inspect the S3 artifact bucket to confirm file presence and timestamps. If an action reports access errors, check the IAM role policies and CloudTrail for access denial events. Another useful strategy is to run a manual build in CodeBuild with the same repository revision; this isolates build-time errors from pipeline orchestration errors. Common issues include syntactic errors in buildspec. yml, missing dependencies during the install phase, and artifacts uploaded to an unexpected base-directory. Document your troubleshooting steps and reproduce failures locally when possible to iterate quickly toward a fix. Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Monitoring
Troubleshooting Checklist
  1. Open CodePipeline to find the failing stage and action details.
  2. Open the corresponding CodeBuild build and read the full logs to identify failing phase and commands.
  3. Check the S3 artifact bucket to confirm the expected files were uploaded after the build.
  4. If AccessDenied appears, inspect the IAM role attached to the failing action for missing permissions.
Practice
When a failure occurs, run the same revision in CodeBuild directly. This isolates build commands from pipeline orchestration and clarifies whether the issue is build logic or pipeline configuration.
Log Focus
Check the install phase first for missing dependencies, then build phase for compile errors, and post-build for packaging problems.
Key Takeaway

Use logs and artifact inspection to narrow issues quickly. Re-run builds in CodeBuild to isolate and fix failing commands before adjusting pipeline wiring.

screens.title: Hands-on Pipeline Creation — Step Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Follow this checklist to assemble a working CI/CD pipeline. Step one, create a CodeCommit repository and push index. html and buildspec. yml in the repository root. Step two, create an IAM role for CodeBuild with policies that allow reading CodeCommit and writing to your artifact S3 bucket. Step three, create a CodeBuild project pointing to the repository and using the buildspec in the repo. Step four, create a CodePipeline pipeline with a source action from CodeCommit, a build action pointing to your CodeBuild project, and a deploy action such as CodeDeploy that reuses the application and deployment group from the prior chapter. Step five, push a small change to index. html and observe the pipeline trigger automatically. As you test, run a manual build in CodeBuild to debug any failing buildspec commands. If the deployment doesn't update your EC2 instance, check the deploy group and the pushed artifact version in the pipeline. This checklist turns conceptual steps into a repeatable workflow you can practice and iterate on. Checklist

screens.title: Common Pipeline Errors and Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring errors appear when building pipelines. First, syntax errors in buildspec. yml such as incorrect indentation or invalid YAML will cause CodeBuild to fail early; validate YAML locally or use a linter before pushing. Second, incorrect artifact patterns or base-directory values produce empty artifacts passed to the deploy stage; after a build, check S3 contents and timestamps to ensure the expected zip or files exist. Third, permission problems happen when service roles lack access to source or artifact buckets; examine the role policies and the pipeline failure message for AccessDenied hints. Fourth, missing runtime dependencies occur when the install phase does not install required packages; ensure you declare runtime versions and explicit install commands. To fix these issues, run a manual build in CodeBuild with full logs and iterate on the buildspec commands, then re-run the pipeline once the build is stable. Keep a tight feedback loop: small commits, test builds, inspect logs, and adjust. That workflow shortens mean-time-to-fix and gives you confidence in pipeline stability. Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Errors & Fixes
Typical Failures
  • buildspec YAML errors: Use a YAML linter; small indentation mistakes break parsing.
  • Artifacts empty: Wrong base-directory or files pattern causes empty S3 uploads.
  • Permission denied: Missing S3 or CodeCommit permissions on the service role.
  • Missing dependencies: Install required packages in the install phase to avoid runtime errors.
Quick Debug
Re-run a failing build manually, read logs for the failing command, and fix buildspec entries. Then retry the pipeline when the build succeeds.
Key Takeaway

Logs and S3 artifact inspection are your fastest path to the root cause. Iterate on buildspec and role policies until runs succeed consistently.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important ideas to carry forward. First, Continuous Integration provides rapid feedback by running automated builds and tests on frequent merges. Second, Continuous Delivery ensures each successful build is packaged and ready to deploy, making releases routine and low-risk. Third, AWS CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline each play a distinct role: source control, build automation with buildspec. yml, and orchestration of stages and artifacts. Fourth, artifacts and service roles are the glue between stages: define artifact paths correctly and grant minimal necessary permissions. Finally, for troubleshooting, the pipeline console points to failing stages and CodeBuild logs reveal command-level errors. Practice the hands-on sequence of creating a repository, adding a buildspec, creating a build project and a pipeline, and then pushing a change to observe the full flow. These steps convert theoretical CI/CD benefits into reliable, reproducible deployments.

Three, use the pipeline console for stage-level failures and CodeBuild logs for command-level errors; run manual builds to isolate failures. These habits reduce time spent on break-fix cycles and make your CI/CD process dependable. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore how Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery reduce friction in software delivery by automatically building, testing, and preparing releases. You will learn what CI and CD mean in practice, how AWS CodeCommit stores your source, how CodeBuild compiles and tests, and how CodePipeline orchestrates stages from source to deploy. I will show a practical workflow that starts with a commit and ends with an automated deployment, and explain why artifacts, build specifications, and IAM roles are vital pieces that hold the pipeline together. You will see a concise hands-on example where a small static site is pushed, built, packaged, and delivered to an EC2 instance through CodeDeploy. Along the way we'll point out common pitfalls, like missing artifacts or incorrect IAM permissions, and how to check build logs when something fails. By the end you should understand the responsibility of each managed service and how a well-formed buildspec file enables reliable, repeatable builds. Think of this chapter as mapping the path from a developer's commit to a safe, repeatable release.

By the end of this chapter you will explain the core ideas of Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery, configure AWS CodeCommit as a secure Git source, author a buildspec file that drives CodeBuild, assemble a multi-stage pipeline in CodePipeline, and monitor or troubleshoot executions and build failures. These objectives are practical: you won't just name services, you'll use CodeCommit to host code, create a CodeBuild project that runs tests and produces artifacts, and link those into a CodePipeline that automates releases. For example, configuring a buildspec file ensures every build follows the same install, pre-build, build and post-build steps so test results are consistent. Another objective is writing minimal IAM roles to allow CodeBuild and CodePipeline to read and write artifacts, which avoids common permission errors. Finally, you will learn monitoring patterns, such as checking CodeBuild logs for failing commands and inspecting the pipeline stage history when a run halts. These skills make deployments predictable and reduce downtime during releases.

These objectives focus on practical outcomes you can perform in the console and terminal. You will create a CodeCommit repository and push application files, write a buildspec file that installs dependencies and runs tests, and configure a CodeBuild project that outputs artifacts to an S3 artifact store. You will also create a CodePipeline pipeline linking source, build, and deploy stages, then validate the whole flow by changing a single H T M L file and watching the automatic release. A concrete check is running a test build in CodeBuild and reading its build logs to confirm the install and build commands executed as expected. Another check is confirming the expected artifact appears in S3 and is passed to the deploy stage. By practicing these steps you’ll learn where to look when a pipeline fails and how to fix common misconfigurations. These practical abilities ensure you move from understanding concepts to operating a working CI/CD pipeline.

Continuous Integration is a development practice where developers frequently merge code changes into a shared repository so an automated build and test suite runs on every merge. The key benefit is fast feedback: integration defects surface quickly when small changes are validated often. Continuous Delivery builds on CI by ensuring that every successful build produces a packaged artifact ready for deployment, so the application is always in a deployable state. In other words, CI answers the question 'Does the code integrate correctly?', while CD answers 'Can this build be safely released to production?'. A practical example is a team that pushes daily updates to a central repository: CI runs tests on each push; CD packages the successful build and makes it available to deployment stages. A common misconception is thinking CI alone equals automated releases; CI only verifies integration, while CD adds the packaging and delivery guarantees. Keep in mind that both practices reduce risk, but CD requires extra steps such as artifact management and deployment automation. To test your grasp, ask: after a passing build, how quickly could you deploy the produced artifact if needed?

AWS provides a managed trio that covers source control, build automation, and orchestration. CodeCommit is the Git-compatible repository that acts as the single source of truth for your code and buildspec files. CodeBuild consumes that source, runs a build environment, executes the commands you author in a buildspec file, and produces artifacts such as a zipped application bundle. CodePipeline wires these pieces together: it defines stages and actions, monitors repository changes, and moves artifacts from source to build, test and deploy stages. A concrete example is when a developer pushes code with a buildspec at the repository root: CodePipeline detects the change, invokes CodeBuild which runs install and test commands and uploads the output artifact to S3. CodePipeline then triggers the deploy action to send the artifact to CodeDeploy or another deployment mechanism. A common mistake is treating CodePipeline as a build server; it is an orchestrator and relies on build services or actions to do the actual compile and test work. Remember to think in terms of artifacts flowing between stages; each service has a focused responsibility that together creates a robust CI/CD flow.

The buildspec file is the contract that tells CodeBuild how to build and package your project. It is a YAML file placed at the repository root and typically declares the version, phases such as install, pre_build, build and post_build, and an artifacts section that lists files to keep. A clear buildspec reduces flakiness by ensuring the build environment runs the same commands every time. For example, for a Node. js app you specify a node runtime, run dependency installation in install, run tests in pre_build, compile in build, and package outputs in post_build. A common mistake is leaving out the base-directory or the files pattern in artifacts, which results in no files being passed downstream. Another pitfall is assuming the build environment includes global tools; you should install or configure needed tools in the install phase. To validate a buildspec, run a test build in CodeBuild and inspect the logs line-by-line. In short, treat buildspec. yml as an exact script for reproducible builds and verify artifact paths to ensure pipeline continuity. Understanding buildspec.yml means buildspec.yml scripts the build environment and the artifact outputs; correct phase commands and artifact patterns are essential for reliable pipelines.. In practical terms, phases, artifacts, and why structure matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Constructing a pipeline means defining stages and actions that move artifacts from source to deployment. The minimal pipeline has three stages: Source, Build, and Deploy. First, create a CodeCommit repository and push your application and buildspec file. Next, create a CodeBuild project configured to use that repository and the buildspec file; set artifacts to an S3 bucket. Finally, create a CodePipeline pipeline that uses CodeCommit as the source action, your CodeBuild project as the build action, and a deploy action such as CodeDeploy pointing at an existing application and deployment group. A concrete CLI example is creating a repository with the cloud CLI and then cloning locally to push code; after pushing, CodePipeline will detect changes and trigger the build. A frequent oversight is not assigning service roles with permissions for S3 or CodeCommit; the pipeline will fail with permission denied errors. After creating the pipeline, trigger a change and observe the execution in the pipeline console. The pipeline will stop on failure, giving you the exact stage and action to investigate. Ask: are artifacts reaching S3 as expected before the deploy stage runs?

In this hands-on step you will create a CodeCommit repository and add the minimal files needed to trigger a pipeline. The repository stores index. html and a buildspec that instructs CodeBuild how to produce an artifact. The activity begins by creating the repository with the CLI, then cloning it locally and adding two files: a basic index. html that serves as the application, and a buildspec. yml that runs a simple static site build. A concrete example is the static site where index. html contains a small message and the buildspec has install and build phases that are effectively no-ops but ensure the pipeline exercise runs. After committing and pushing, CodePipeline will detect the change and start a run if the pipeline is configured. Watch for permission errors on push; ensure your Git credentials for CodeCommit are set up. This exercise teaches the end-to-end trigger: a single push can initiate the whole CI/CD flow when the pipeline is wired correctly. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Artifacts are the tangible outputs of build steps: compiled code, packages, Docker images, or static web files. In AWS pipelines, CodeBuild produces artifacts according to the buildspec's artifacts section and typically uploads them to an S3 artifact bucket. CodePipeline actions consume those artifacts as inputs for subsequent stages. For example, CodeBuild might package a site into a zip file and place it in a named S3 bucket; the deploy action then references that artifact to update the target environment. A common error is misconfiguring the artifacts. files or base-directory in buildspec. yml so the expected files are not included, resulting in empty inputs for the deploy stage. Another gotcha is S3 permissions: ensure the pipeline and build roles can write to and read from the artifact bucket. When diagnosing issues, verify the S3 bucket contains the expected artifact after a successful build and examine the pipeline execution history to confirm the artifact version passed along. Clear artifact paths and permissions keep stages connected and deployments reliable. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Monitoring pipeline health requires looking at the right places: the CodePipeline console for the high-level execution flow and the CodeBuild logs for command-level detail. When a pipeline run fails at a stage, the pipeline console tells you which action failed and often includes an error summary. For build failures, open the CodeBuild build details and read the full logs to see which phase and command produced the error. For missing artifacts, inspect the S3 artifact bucket to confirm file presence and timestamps. If an action reports access errors, check the IAM role policies and CloudTrail for access denial events. Another useful strategy is to run a manual build in CodeBuild with the same repository revision; this isolates build-time errors from pipeline orchestration errors. Common issues include syntactic errors in buildspec. yml, missing dependencies during the install phase, and artifacts uploaded to an unexpected base-directory. Document your troubleshooting steps and reproduce failures locally when possible to iterate quickly toward a fix. Several recurring errors appear when building pipelines. First, syntax errors in buildspec. yml such as incorrect indentation or invalid YAML will cause CodeBuild to fail early; validate YAML locally or use a linter before pushing. Second, incorrect artifact patterns or base-directory values produce empty artifacts passed to the deploy stage; after a build, check S3 contents and timestamps to ensure the expected zip or files exist. Third, permission problems happen when service roles lack access to source or artifact buckets; examine the role policies and the pipeline failure message for AccessDenied hints. Fourth, missing runtime dependencies occur when the install phase does not install required packages; ensure you declare runtime versions and explicit install commands. To fix these issues, run a manual build in CodeBuild with full logs and iterate on the buildspec commands, then re-run the pipeline once the build is stable. Keep a tight feedback loop: small commits, test builds, inspect logs, and adjust. That workflow shortens mean-time-to-fix and gives you confidence in pipeline stability. Let's summarize the most important ideas to carry forward. First, Continuous Integration provides rapid feedback by running automated builds and tests on frequent merges. Second, Continuous Delivery ensures each successful build is packaged and ready to deploy, making releases routine and low-risk. Third, AWS CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline each play a distinct role: source control, build automation with buildspec. yml, and orchestration of stages and artifacts. Fourth, artifacts and service roles are the glue between stages: define artifact paths correctly and grant minimal necessary permissions. Finally, for troubleshooting, the pipeline console points to failing stages and CodeBuild logs reveal command-level errors. Keep these three reminders close as you work on pipelines. One, define a clear buildspec that lists install, test, build, and artifact output steps so builds are repeatable. Two, ensure artifacts are uploaded correctly and that the pipeline and build roles have permission to read and write them; missing artifacts are a frequent cause of pipeline failures. Three, use the pipeline console for stage-level failures and CodeBuild logs for command-level errors; run manual builds to isolate failures. These habits reduce time spent on break-fix cycles and make your CI/CD process dependable.
